text:
IN THE SUPREME
COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

J.S.
v.
G.J.S.
,

2005 BCSC 1373

Date: 20051005

Docket:
EO10826

Registry:
Vancouver

Between:

J.S.

Plaintiff

And

G.J.S.

Defendant

Before:
The Honourable Mr. Justice Rice

Reasons for Judgment

The Plaintiff:

In
Person

Counsel for the Defendant:

Ms. H.
Cunningham

Date and Place of Trial:

September
6, 7, 8, 9, 12, 13, 14 and 15, 2005

Vancouver,
B.C.

[
1
]

This action is a custody battle over the two
children of these parties. The children are D.S., age 7, and A.S., age 5.  The
parties separated shortly after A.S. was born after three-and-a-half years of
marriage.

[
2
]

The plaintiff father, Mr. J.S., seeks joint
custody and guardianship with each parent having the children every other week.
He also seeks a permanent order in the form of the Police Clause added by order
of September 3, 2003.

[
3
]

The defendant mother, Ms. G.J.S., wants sole
custody and guardianship, allowing the father no change in the current status
of access which is mainly every other weekend plus stipulated dates and daily
telephone access. The defendant also seeks a permanent order to restrain the
plaintiff from contacting the defendant or the children on the terms granted as
an interim injunction and later modified in the action.

[
4
]

Both parties claim child and spousal support.

[
5
]

Mr. J.S. is a manufacturer’s representative born
[…], 1949, in Morocco where he lived to the age of 13. He and his family then
moved to Israel. He immigrated to Canada at the age of 23 in 1971.  He has
lived in Canada ever since and resides in a one-bedroom apartment in Vancouver,
B.C.  He now pays $7.00 per month for child support and $50.00 per month for
spousal support.

[
6
]

Ms. G.J.S. is a fitness trainer born in British
Columbia.  She grew up in Nanaimo and now lives with the two children at her
parents’ home in Langley. They have lived there since about May 2001.

[
7
]

The parties met in 1996 and married May 7,
1997.  They lived together in a comfortable, newer condominium apartment in
Vancouver.  Mr. J.S. worked as a clothing manufacturer’s representative selling
substantial quantities of clothing through a holding company called S.[…].  He
was fairly successful at that time it would seem.  He had been in the business
for over 20 years.  Ms. G.J.S. worked as a sales representative for Sunlight
Juice.

[
8
]

Early in the marriage, Ms. G.J.S. suffered a
miscarriage.  Soon after that she became pregnant again and bore a son, D.S.,
on […], 1998.  She ceased working outside the home a few months before. After
the birth, she suffered a post-partum depression. It seems that this was the
time when strife developed between the couple.

[
9
]

Neither admits any fault and both blame the
other for this discord.  He says that she left him to do nearly all of the work
around the home including caring for the child. He was also trying to run his
business. She testified that his behaviour changed, and he became extremely
emotional, aggressive, and demanding.  He would have fits of temper where he
would heap verbal abuse on her and sometimes pound his fists on doors,
cupboards, and walls. He denies that for the most part, except once when he
knocked a hole in their bathroom wall.

[
10
]

The second son, A.S., was born […], 2000.  In
July 2000, the family moved to Montreal where they hoped to improve Mr. J.S.’s fortunes
in business. Ms. G.J.S. went along, hoping that it would also make for improvement
in their troubled relationship.  Unfortunately, the relationship did not
improve in Montreal.  It became worse.

[
11
]

In October 2000, while Mr. J.S. was at work, Ms.
G.J.S. left their apartment with the children to stay elsewhere and reported to
the police that he had threatened her.  As a result, he was charged with
assault and was placed under an injunction not to contact his wife or
children.  Mr. J.S. did not see his children again for eight months.

[
12
]

Not long after the charges were laid, Mr. J.S.
moved back to British Columbia because the opportunities in Montreal were not
turning out as he hoped.  Ms. G.J.S. stayed in Montreal with the children until
mid-May 2001, when Mr. J.S.’s trial for criminal assault against her took
place. He was acquitted.  After the trial, Ms. G.J.S. moved back to British
Columbia as well and went to live with her parents in Langley.  The stage was
then set for the ensuing bitter relations between the parties over Mr. J.S.’s
access to the children.  They have led to no fewer than nine court orders.

[
13
]

By order of Master Barber June 27, 2001, sole
interim custody and guardianship of the children was granted to Ms. G.J.S..  Mr.
J.S. was granted supervised access once per week for three hours, and after two
weeks, twice per week for three hours each.  An order was made for preparation
of a report under
s. 15
of the
Family Relations Act,
R.S.B.C.
1996, c. 128 [
F.R.A.
]
.
Master Barber also ordered
that Mr. J.S. be restrained from contacting or harassing Ms. G.J.S. or the
children, and that the children not be removed from the Lower Mainland of
British Columbia by either party without further order the court.  Mr. J.S. was
also ordered to pay child support of $7.00 a month (the guideline amount for
his income level of $7,000 per year) and $50.00 a month in spousal support.

[
14
]

A report was produced January 10, 2002.  In it,
the author, Dr. Elterman, noted Ms. G.J.S.’s reports of Mr. J.S.’s fits of
temper, and also her fear of the threat that he would abduct the children and
take them to Israel.  Dr. Elterman seemed to agree that Mr. J.S. was at least
“excitable”.  Dr. Elterman’s testing and interviews led him to suggest that
anxiety, tension, and depression more than anger were the cause.  He expressed
the need for Mr. J.S. to come to an understanding of his tendencies to react
emotionally and without reflection.  He did not accept Ms. G.J.S.’s suggestion
that Mr. J.S.’s behaviour indicated a likely chance of physical violence or abduction
of the children. He said that both parents demonstrated overwhelmingly positive
feelings towards the children.

[
15
]

Dr. Elterman also considered Mr. J.S.’s proposal
for equal sharing of the children. Dr. Elterman cautioned that the move into
longer and unsupervised access for Mr. J.S. needed to be taken more slowly due
to the children’s ages and partly due to the lack of familiarity that had
developed since the separation. He recommended that the parents work with a
counsellor and/or mediator, and that Mr. J.S. have unsupervised access every
Saturday or Sunday during the day with an additional three-hour period possibly
on Wednesdays.

[
16
]

On May 15, 2002, Master Barber varied his
previous order of June 27, 2001.  He granted unsupervised access to Mr. J.S.
every Saturday from 1:30 p.m. to 6:30 p.m. for two months and following that
from 11:30 a.m. to 6:30 p.m. plus from 3:30 p.m. to 6:30 p.m. on Wednesdays.
He also varied the restraining order to allow the parties to communicate and
have contact with one another regarding access for emergency purposes, exchange
of the children, and for the purpose of mediation. Those parts of the previous
order not varied remained in effect as before.

[
17
]

On November 18, 2002, Mr. Justice Groberman
varied the access order to provide for Mr. J.S. to have overnight access one
night per month, and after three months, one night every other week.  On the
non-overnight weekends, he was also granted Saturday access from 9:00 a.m. to
7:00 p.m.

[
18
]

On December 20, 2002, Mr. Justice Warren granted
the parties a divorce.

[
19
]

From the time that he obtained unsupervised
access in 2002, Mr. J.S. would appear at the access exchange locations and
cause scenes that were frightening and that disrupted the exchange process. He
would at times yell at Ms G.J.S., accusing her of poisoning the family.  He
even spit at her at least once and smashed her tape recorder another time. I
will not elaborate further on the details of these events, which regularly
occurred at these exchanges with the result that the children were confused and
crying. On a number of occasions the police had to intervene because of the
disorder. In fact, the point of exchange was changed to the parking lot of the
R.C.M.P. detachment in view of the problems.

[
20
]

On June 13, 2003, Mr. Justice McEwan ordered
that on the exchange of the children for access purposes, the parties were to record
and keep available the recordings for the court.  He also ordered an updated
report from Dr. Elterman.

[
21
]

On July 30, 2003, Mr. Justice McEwan ordered
that Mr. J.S. have the children from August 23 to August 30, 2003.

[
22
]

On September 5, 2003, Mr. Justice McEwan ordered
that Mr. J.S. have access to the children from September 5 to October 5, 2003,
with regular access to resume thereafter.  He further ordered that Mr. J.S.
have reasonable telephone access.  Finally, he ordered that should Ms. G.J.S.
deny access to Mr. J.S., the police were authorized to arrest Ms. G.J.S., take
custody of the children, and turn them over to their father. This was the
result of an unfortunate episode where Mr. J.S. was wrongly placed under
suspicion and investigated for sexual abuse of the children.  In the midst of
that investigation, Ms. G.J.S. refused to grant access.  She was arrested and
gave up the children as ordered.  After that month, the parties returned to the
previously ordered access arrangement.

[
23
]

During the summer of 2004, or part of it, Mr.
J.S. had access to the children every other week by agreement.

[
24
]

On April 3, 2005, Master Keighley ordered the
dismissal of an application by Mr. J.S. for sole custody and ordered costs
against him in any event.

[
25
]

On June 2, 2005, Madam Justice Neilson ordered
access for Mr. J.S. on Father’s Day, June 11, 2005, and also telephone access
from 7:00 p.m. to 7:15 p.m. every day when the children were not with him.

[
26
]

On July 19, 2005, Mr. Justice Burnyeat granted Mr.
J.S. access from July 29 to August 30, 2005.

[
27
]

Meanwhile, Dr. Elterman provided two further
updates, one on March 20, 2004, and another on July 13, 2005.  Dr. Elterman
says in his last report:

What is remarkable about this case is the
length of time that this has remained a high-conflict case.  It has been a few
years since Ms. G.J.S. and Mr. J.S. separated and the level of mistrust and
animosity has continued at problematic levels.  From a review of the documents
provided and my two previous reports, it is clear that they each see themselves
as the victim of the other party.

[
28
]

The evidence leads me to share that view.

[
29
]

Although Mr. J.S. denies it, I accept as fact Ms.
G.J.S.’s testimony in regard to his volatile, aggressive behaviour.  She gave
straightforward evidence on several examples. Her evidence was corroborated by the
testimony of her mother and her fiancé, who were eyewitnesses on some occasions,
and whom I consider to be credible.  It was also corroborated by two
independent witnesses, Ms. Tan and Ms. Oldaker, who witnessed episodes of Mr.
J.S.’s loss of temper.  I find that on most of the exchanges his behaviour was
out of control.  Although he committed no physical harm, his behaviour was very
frightening to the children and Ms. G.J.S..

[
30
]

Mr. J.S.’s several denials of the allegations of
the defendant’s witnesses as to these episodes, and his own versions, I do not
find credible, and I reject them.

[
31
]

It is important to say that this tendency of Mr.
J.S.’s towards aggressiveness does not seem to characterize any of his
behaviour directly towards the children during his access weekends.  By all
accounts, he is a very good parent and treats the children very well.

[
32
]

Dr. Elterman in his report indicated that the access
exchange confrontations were stressful to the children and not good for them.
The arrangement of making the exchanges at a police station may be useful and
necessary if the parties are involved directly, but it creates the expectation
possibly in the children’s minds that the undertaking is dangerous and requires
the police to accomplish it.

[
33
]

Dr. Elterman gave the opinion that the
children’s physical and emotional needs are well taken care of by Ms. G.J.S.
and her parents.  They have a comfortable home, and provide a good nurturing
atmosphere.  Ms. G.J.S. is now engaged to be married to another man, A.W., who
owns his own business and has his own comfortable home in the area.  Ms. G.J.S.
plans to move there with the children in due course.  I was impressed by Mr.
A.W. as an honest, steady, capable, and compassionate person who gets along
with the children very well.

[
34
]

At the same time, Dr. Elterman expressed the
view that “there remains a passive-aggressive approach in Mr. J.S.’s relationship
with the children on [Ms. G.J.S.’s] part.  Mr. J.S. is someone who presents at
his proverbial wits’ end and is frustrated and angry by what he sees as years
of provocation.”  I share Dr. Elterman’s impression.

[
35
]

Although I accept Ms. G.J.S.’s evidence that Mr.
J.S.’s unpredictable and frequent outbursts of temper and acts of violence,
such as pounding a hole in the wall, are very frightening to her, and may
justify her strong wish to stay right away from him, she has reacted at times
out of spite and not just fright. In her testimony, she showed an attitude of
scorn toward him, accusing him of abandoning his children and saying that he
doesn’t love his children. That view is unwarranted and unfair, and I have
little doubt that she has unnecessarily provoked Mr. J.S.’s anger by displays
of this attitude.

[
36
]

On this point, I asked Dr. Elterman whether the
past separations of Mr. J.S. from his children, and the continuing problems with
access, have created an element of alienation in his relationship with the
children.  Dr. Elterman answered that he did not believe that this was a case
of alienation.  He had seen Mr. J.S. with the children and noted that when they
are alone and settled down from the exchange, they get along in a normal way.
What may seem to be alienation to Mr. J.S. is more likely a reaction by the
children in some cases to the negativity of the transfers.  Episodes of one or
the other child refusing to come with him, or crying, can be eliminated by
eliminating the confrontation.

[
37
]

The parties have each applied for custody of the
children under both the
federal
Divorce
Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 3 [
Divorce

Act] and the provincial
F.R.A.
Both acts govern custody
and access disputes in the British Columbia Supreme Court.  This overlapping
jurisdiction exists because of the division of powers set out in the
Constitution

Act, 1867.

[
38
]

Whereas the
F.R.A.
has broader
applicability, the
Divorce Act
applies only to custody disputes where,
as here, the parents also petition for divorce. Even though a divorce has been
granted, the court continues to have jurisdiction to determine custody disputes
under the
Divorce Act
as long as one of the former spouses is
ordinarily resident in the province or both former spouses accept the court’s
jurisdiction (
s. 4(1)
).

[
39
]

Section 16
of the
Divorce Act
, expressly
mandates that the best interests of the child is the only consideration in a
custody or access dispute. The court must determine “best interests” by
assessing “the condition, means, needs and other circumstances of the child”
(
s. 16(8)
). Parliament singled out only two factors of special importance to
guide the court in its assessment: First, the court is forbidden to consider the
past conduct of a parent unless that conduct is relevant to the person’s
parenting ability (s. 16(9)). Second, the court must ensure that a child has as
much contact with each parent as is consistent with that child’s best
interests. In applying this principle of maximum contact, the court must
consider the willingness of the person seeking custody to facilitate such
contact (s. 16(10)).

[
40
]

The
F.R.A.
differs from the
Divorce
Act
in four fundamental ways:

•

The
F.R.A.
characterizes the best
interests of the child as the “paramount” rather than the “only” consideration
in a custody or access dispute (
s. 24(1)
).

•

The
F.R.A
. provides more detailed
guidance regarding the content of the best interests analysis. Specifically,
the
F.R.A.
mandates that the court consider the child’s health
and emotional well being, the child’s views (where appropriate), the bond
between the child and other significant persons, the child’s education and
training, and the ability of each person granted guardianship, custody, or
access to fulfil those duties (s.24(1)(a) – (e)).

•

While the
F.R.A
. also prohibits
the court from considering parental conduct that does not affect the child’s
interests, the restriction is not limited to past conduct as it is in the
Divorce
Act

(
s. 24(3)
). Rather, the court may consider present and future
conduct only in so far as the conduct affects one of the listed factors set out
in the legislation (s.24(4)).

•

The
F.R.A.

does not include an
express principle of maximum contact between parent and child consistent with
that child’s best interests.

[
41
]

In practice these differences in the language of
the two acts do not lead to collisions because neither act attempts to set out
an exhaustive or formulaic set of criteria for determining the best interests
of a child (
Young v. Young
,
1993 CanLII 34 (SCC)
, [1993] 4 S.C.R. 3, 49 R.F.L. (3d) 117
at para.
203
,
Anson v. Anson

(1987), 10 B.C.L.R. (2d) 357, [1987]
B.C.J. No. 127 (Co. Ct.)
). On the contrary, the best interests enquiry is
deliberately wide-ranging under both acts (
King v. Low
,
1985 CanLII 59 (SCC)
, [1985] 1
S.C.R. 87, 44 R.F.L. (2d) 113 at para.
29
). The courts have emphasized under
both acts a variety of factors including the importance of stability in a
child’s life, the security of the parents’ environment, and the child’s
physical, emotional, intellectual, and spiritual development.  (
Poole v.
Poole
(1999), 64 B.C.L.R. (3d) 70,
1999 BCCA 203
at para.
22
).

[
42
]

Because each child is entitled to individual
justice, the courts must undertake the best interests analysis free of any
legal or factual presumptions, including any presumption either in favour or
against joint custody orders (
Robinson v. Filyk
(1996),
1996 CanLII 3310 (BC CA)
, 28
B.C.L.R. (3d) 21, 84 B.C.A.C. 290 (C.A.) at paras
22 and 27
) "Each case
turns on its own unique circumstances and the only issue is the best interests
of the child in the particular circumstances of the case" (
Gordon v.
Goertz,
1996 CanLII 191 (SCC)
, [1996] 2 S.C.R. 27 at 59 – 60, 19 R.F.L. (4
th
) 177).

[
43
]

Mr. J.S. now seeks joint custody with equal
parenting time. Ms. G.J.S. argues that the children would be better off if she
continues to have sole custody with access to Mr. J.S. as previously ordered.

[
44
]

The term “custody” is not defined in either the
Divorce
Act

or the
F.R.A.
; however, over time, the jurisprudence
has developed both broad and narrow definitions. In its narrow sense, custody
describes the day-to-day physical care and control of a child. This definition
appears to have given way to a broader meaning that encompasses not only
physical control but also the responsibility to make decisions regarding the
intellectual, emotional, and spiritual upbringing of a child. This broader
definition includes the concept of guardianship and grants the custodial parent
“the right to exercise full parental authority” over the child (
Young v. Young
,
supra
at para.
24
,
Anson v. Anson,
supra
).

[
45
]

Section 27(4)
of the
F.R.A.

specifies
that when sole custody is ordered under the
Divorce Act
, the
custodial parent is also the sole guardian of the child. An order for sole
custody, therefore, empowers the custodial parent to make all significant
decisions affecting the child’s education, health, religion, and activities.

[
46
]

If the non-custodial parent is granted access to
the child, that parent will have the right to spend time with the child away
from the custodial parent and will necessarily have responsibility for the
child’s care during the access period.  The Supreme Court of Canada has
explained that access is intended to facilitate a meaningful, continuing,
post-divorce relationship between the children of the marriage and the access
parent (
Young v. Young
, supra
at para.
179 and 205
).

To
that end, access parents may share their religion, lifestyle, and other
important aspects of themselves with their children to the extent that this is
consistent with the children’s best interests. However, the access parent may
not interfere with the custodial parent’s decisions regarding the child’s
upbringing (
Anson v. Anson
,
supra
at 368).

[
47
]

In contrast, an order for joint custody provides
that both parents continue to share the authority and responsibility for
decisions relating to the child’s upbringing just as they did prior to their
separation. Such an order may include an order for equal, or nearly equal,
parenting time and regular changes of residence, but does not necessarily
include these features. Because the authority to make decisions for the child
is shared, joint custody necessitates at least a certain degree of consultation
and cooperation between the separating parents (
Lucken v. Hopkins

(1994),
1994 CanLII 325 (BC CA)
, 8 R.F.L. (4
th
) 226, [1994] B.C.J. No. 2125 (C.A.);
Ness
v. Ness
(1999), 43 R.F.L. (4
th
) 363,
1999 BCCA 51
).

[
48
]

Although an order for joint custody may be made
in situations where the parents have difficulty communicating with one another
(see
P.Y.Y.M. v. D.M.
,
2003 BCSC 766
, [2003] B.C.J. No. 1149, and

Carr v. Carr
,
2001 BCCA 415
, [2001] B.C.J. No. 1219), I do
not believe that such an order would be in the best interests of the children
in this case. The parties have been consistently unable to prevent the tension,
confusion and strife over access exchanges.  The result has been trauma to the
children.  Mr. J.S. and Ms. G.J.S. cannot communicate with one another without
rancour and have been unable to implement shared parenting or agree on an
access schedule without frequent recourse to the courts. Consequently, I see
little prospect for the co-operation, consultation, and joint decision-making
that is necessary to make joint custody workable. In light of this animosity, a
joint custody order likely would increase opportunities for conflict, exposing
the children to greater stress.

[
49
]

Dr. Elterman recommended an arrangement whereby Mr.
J.S. would care for the children every other week from Wednesday afternoon to
Monday morning (five days).

[
50
]

I agree that this would be a good solution from
the standpoint of allowing Mr. J.S. larger blocks of time to build his
relationship with the children.  But I have two reservations which cause me to
find that such an arrangement would not be in the children’s best interests at
this time.  The first reason is that the children go to school in Langley, and Mr.
J.S. would be put to driving them back and forth (over 45 to 90 minutes each
way every school day that he has them).  The children, D.S., age 7, and A.S.,
age 5, are young, and that kind of travel back and forth would be difficult for
them.  Of course, this difficulty would be overcome if Mr. J.S. moved to
Langley or nearby.

[
51
]

However, my major reservation is not the travel
inconvenience.  It is my concern with the emotional stability of Mr. J.S..  His
behaviour at the exchanges, the yelling, the accusations, the threats, locking
himself inside his vehicle so as not to let the children get in, were so often
terribly traumatic to the children, and I have a concern that before long they
will be witnessing this kind of behaviour at home with him. I have no reason to
expect, on the evidence, that he would do any harm to the children.  But the
outbursts of temper of themselves have been so frightening to adults that have
witnessed them that I have a serious concern that there is a risk of psychological
harm to the children

[
52
]

Mr. J.S.’s lack of insight into his own
aggressive behaviour (which he terms merely “excitable”) and its detrimental
effect on the children leads me to conclude that the current arrangement,
subject to some adjustments, is optimum.  More access now for Mr. J.S. would
not be in their best interests.  In my opinion the current arrangement provides
enough access so that these children can have the chance to know their father.
I believe that what I will order is reasonably accommodating of that goal.

[
53
]

Ms. G.J.S. has been the children’s primary
caregiver.  She has the ability to provide a stable, comfortable home for the
children.  Both boys are closely bonded to her and to her parents with whom
they now live and who have assisted with childcare for many years.

[
54
]

Preserving more time in the children’s stable
environment in Langley will help to compensate for stress during exchanges and
their parents mutual animosity. It will give Mr. J.S. more time to recover
financially and to seek more counselling for management of his anger. That is
the best solution for now.

[
55
]

I order that Ms. G.J.S. shall continue to have
sole custody and sole guardianship of the children and that their primary
residence shall be with her.  I order that Mr. J.S. shall have access to the
children every second Friday at the end of their school day, or 3:30 p.m. if
there is no school day, until Monday morning at the start of their school day,
or 9:00 a.m. if there is no school day.  On school days he will pick the
children up at their school and will drop them off at school the following
Monday.  If there is no school when he picks them up or drops them off, he will
pick them up, or drop them off, as the case may be, through a third party to be
named in advance by Ms. G.J.S..  If she does not name a third party, Mr. J.S.
may deliver them to her directly.

[
56
]

Mr. J.S. shall also have access for the day on
his choice of Jewish holidays up to a maximum number of seven days total in any
year, plus his birthday, Father’s Day, and the Monday of any long weekend that
falls on his scheduled weekend of access.  He shall notify Ms. G.J.S. by
January 15 each year of the dates of those holidays that he chooses.

[
57
]

Ms. G.J.S. shall have the children with her on
her birthday, Mother’s Day, and Christmas Day.  If any of these days should
fall during Mr. J.S.’s regular access periods, Mr. J.S. shall have one extra
day on the following weekend in compensation.

[
58
]

Mr. J.S. shall have access to the children in the
month of July commencing this year during the first and third week, and also
for the first two consecutive weeks of August.  The parties shall divide the
school spring break equally between them.

[
59
]

Mr. J.S. shall have access to the children by
telephone on days when the children are with the plaintiff.  Ms. G.J.S. shall
encourage the children to accept Mr. J.S.’s telephone calls and speak with him.

[
60
]

Ms. G.J.S. will have responsibility for the
day-to-day care of the children but will have the obligation to advise Mr. J.S.
in writing of any matters of a significant nature affecting the children.  Mr.
J.S. may submit to Ms. G.J.S. in writing any suggestions or opinions that he
may have in that regard.

[
61
]

Mr. J.S. shall have the right, under
s. 32
of
the
F.R.A.
,

to seek a review of any decision that he
considers contrary to the best interests of either of the children.

[
62
]

Both parents will have the right to obtain information
concerning the children directly from third parties, including teachers,
counsellors, medical professionals, and third party caregivers.

[
63
]

The injunction restraining Mr. J.S. from contact
with Ms. G.J.S. as ordered and modified by Master Barber will continue in
effect.  The order of Mr. Justice McEwan authorizing the police to arrest Ms.
G.J.S. if she fails to allow access as provided in this order will also be
incorporated in this order.

[
64
]

As regards spousal and child support, Ms.
Cunningham, acting for the defendant Ms. G.J.S., calculated that in the years
2001 to 2004, the average total of Mr. J.S.’s income plus 75% of his operating
expenses was $39,925.00 based on Mr. J.S.’s financial reports.

[
65
]

Mr. J.S. has been living on next to nothing,
rent free in an apartment owned by his sister.  He has been paying next to
nothing by way of support for his children.  He claims, and I accept, that his
business has not done well over the past several years, partly because of the
market generally, and partly because one or more specific accounts went sour.
He was left with a large uncollectible receivable on the bankruptcy of one of
his customers.  There is also no doubt that this action and the troubles with Ms.
G.J.S. have distracted him from putting his full energy into his business.

[
66
]

Mr. J.S.’s financial statements disclose some
steady activity over the past five years, however.  Based on the fact that, on
his own evidence, he runs nearly all of his expenses through his company, I do
not have much evidence of what portion of the operating expenses should be
characterized as personal.  However, I agree with Ms. Cunningham, and Mr. J.S.
provided no evidence to the contrary, that there must be some reasonable
portion that should be reallocated.

[
67
]

I would impute a total income of $25,000.00.
According to the latest Federal Child Support tables, that would call for
monthly support payments of $375.00 for these two children, and I so order
effective the 1
st
of the month following this judgment and the 1
st

day of every month afterwards.

[
68
]

In making an order for spousal support, the
court must consider the conditions, means, needs, and other circumstances of
each spouse, including the length of time the spouses cohabited, the role each
spouse played in the relationship, the capacity of each spouse to support
themselves, the custodial obligations of the spouses with respect to their
children, and any order or agreement relating to support that has been made (
Divorce
Act
,
s. 15.2(4),
F.R.A.
, s. 89). Each spouse has a
positive obligation to take reasonable steps to become self-sufficient within a
reasonable amount of time. (
Divorce Act
,
s. 15.2(6),
F.R.A.
,
s. 89(2)).

[
69
]

The purpose of spousal support is “to promote
the equitable sharing of the economic consequences of marriage or marriage
breakdown” (
Moge v. Moge
,
1992 CanLII 25 (SCC)
, [1992] 3 S.C.R. 813, 43 R.F.L. (3d)
345). The fact of marriage alone does not automatically entitle a spouse to
support (
Moge v. Moge
,
supra,
Bracklow v. Bracklow
,
1999 CanLII 715 (SCC)
, [1999]
1 S.C.R. 420, 44 R.F.L. (4
th
) 1).

[
70
]

These parties were married for a comparatively
short time. They cohabited for only about three-and-a-half years. Neither party
presented evidence to substantiate a claim for compensatory support based on
significant economic loss suffered during the marriage.

[
71
]

Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied
that neither of these parties has substantial means from which to make support
payments to the other. I am equally satisfied that neither has great need for
such support. I have already expressed the opinion that with the end of this
litigation, Mr. J.S. will be able to devote more of his energy to developing
his business.  Most likely he will quickly achieve a level of success
sufficient to support himself and meet his child support obligations. Ms.
G.J.S. is now a fitness trainer with a significant private clientele. She will
soon marry Mr. A.W., a man whom I have described as capable and compassionate,
who owns his own business and enjoys a comfortable lifestyle.  While a new
relationship does not automatically disentitle Ms. G.J.S. to spousal support
(see
Boudreau v. Bradbury
(1998),
1998 CanLII 1805 (BC SC)
, 38 R.F.L. (4
th
) 1,
[1998] B.C.J. No. 1007 (B.C.S.C.),

I am satisfied that her new
marriage and her successful business will provide her with a comfortable
lifestyle such that she will not need Mr. J.S.’s support.

[
72
]

I make no order for spousal support to either
party.

[
73
]

Each party will bear its own costs.

“THE
HONOURABLE MR. JUSTICE RICE”
